title: Despair not
hookLine: despair not of God's mercy, for God forgives all sins (Quran 39:53)
carry: even if your sins reached the clouds

lines: AWAKE AT TWO IN THE MORNING.
A VERSE SPOKEN INTO THAT VOICE.
cards: Two in the morning, and somebody is awake, replaying something they did years ago. A word said in anger. A friend let down.
A thing nobody else knows. Others may have forgiven or forgotten it. Not the one lying awake.
There's a voice in that kind of night that says: too late, too much, this one stays. The Qur'an has a verse spoken straight into that voice. It doesn't start with a rule.
It starts by naming the people it's talking to.

teach.h: O MY SLAVES: STILL CALLED MINE.
teach.b: First, who it's for. The verse opens with a command to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, to speak in God's name. In Pickthall's translation: "Say: O My slaves who have been prodigal to their own hurt!"
Prodigal here means people who have gone too far, wasting themselves, hurting their own souls. Notice the word My. Not those people: My slaves, belonging to God.
The ones who went too far are still addressed as His. Second, the command. "Despair not of the mercy of Allah."

What's forbidden, at least in this line, isn't the wrong. It's despair. The verse treats hopelessness about mercy as its own kind of mistake, as if to say the door is not the problem; believing it's locked is.
Third, the reach. "Who forgiveth all sins." All.

teach.h: ALL SINS, AND A TURNING BACK.
teach.b: The next verse calls people to turn to their Lord and surrender to Him before a reckoning comes, and the promise is read together with that turning back. Read that way, mercy isn't a reason to stop caring.
It's a reason not to give up. Fourth, the name.
The verse ends: "Lo! He is the Forgiving, the Merciful." The Forgiving, in Arabic, is al-Ghafur, one of the names Muslims use for God.
A saying of the Prophet, recorded by at-Tirmidhi, puts it vividly: in it God says that even if a person's sins reached the clouds of the sky, and they asked forgiveness, God would forgive them.

teach.h: DESPAIR NOT OF THE MERCY OF ALLAH.
teach.b: For Muslims who pray with this verse, it answers the voice that says too late with two words: despair not.

how: Muslims seek God's forgiveness, called istighfar, in prayer and in their own words, and call on God by names such as al-Ghafur, the Forgiving.

o: the Forgiving: a name Muslims use for God
a title for a teacher who explains the Qur'an
the Arabic word for the call to prayer

games.q: inside the verse — tap the pairs.

s: the verse is addressed to people who never did wrong
it's for those "who have been prodigal to their own hurt," and it calls them My slaves.
the verse ends by naming God the Forgiving, the Merciful
"Lo! He is the Forgiving, the Merciful."
the verse's promise is a reason to stop caring
the next verse calls people to turn to their Lord, and the two are read together.

games.q: the verse speaks to people who have gone too far and hurt their own souls. what's the first thing it tells them not to do?
o: not to pray until they've made amends.
not to despair of God's mercy.
not to speak of what they did.
games.why: "despair not of the mercy of Allah, Who forgiveth all sins." the thing forbidden here is hopelessness.

practice: Let one old guilt come up, something already done that you've said sorry for or can't fix now, and hold it the way the verse holds its listeners: as someone who went too far and is still called by name.
When the voice says it's too late, don't argue; just set the verse's two words beside it, despair not, and let the weight loosen a little, even if it doesn't leave.
If you pray, you can ask forgiveness in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Al-Ghafur. The Forgiving, a name for God in Islam, from the verse that tells those who went too far: despair not. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the Forgiving, as Qur'an 39:53 names God.
